findings.title: New abstract `order()` method breaks existing CryptoProvider implementations
findings.body: `int order();` is added to the public `CryptoProvider` interface as an abstract method. `CryptoProvider` is an SPI that is implemented outside this repository (e.g. the keycloak-client repo, adapters, custom/vendor crypto modules). Any existing implementation that is not recompiled will fail at runtime with `AbstractMethodError` as soon as `CryptoIntegration.detectProvider()` calls `CryptoProvider::order`, and sources will no longer compile. Declaring it as a `default` method (e.g. `default int order() { return 0; }`) would keep the SPI backward compatible while still allowing the authz-client provider to lower/raise its priority.

findings.title: Multiple crypto providers on classpath are no longer rejected; ties resolved nondeterministically and only logged at debug
findings.body: The previous code threw `IllegalStateException` when more than one `CryptoProvider` was found on the classpath. Now the list is sorted by `order()` and the first entry is used silently. All three real providers (`DefaultCryptoProvider`, `FIPS1402Provider`, `WildFlyElytronProvider`) return the same order `200`, so if two of them end up on the same classpath (e.g. BC non-FIPS jar accidentally present in a FIPS deployment) the winner depends on `ServiceLoader` iteration order, and the fact that a provider was ignored is only reported via `logger.debugf` (off by default). That turns a previously loud, deterministic failure into a silent, non-deterministic choice of crypto backend — in a FIPS deployment it can mean silently running with non-approved crypto. At minimum, equal-order collisions should still fail (or be logged at WARN) rather than being resolved arbitrarily.

findings.title: `logger.debugf(String)` used as a format string with no arguments and built unconditionally
findings.body: `logger.debugf(builder.toString())` resolves to the varargs `debugf(String format, Object... params)` overload with an empty parameter array, so the message is passed through `String.format`. Any `%` character in the message (class names normally have none, but the message is data-driven) would raise `UnknownFormatConversionException`/`MissingFormatArgumentException` from a logging call. In addition, the `StringBuilder` is populated and `toString()` is invoked even when debug logging is disabled. Use `logger.debug(...)` (optionally guarded by `isDebugEnabled()`), or a proper format string with parameters.

findings.title: Dead statements in concatenatedRSToASN1DER
findings.body: Lines 114-115 (`ASN1Encoder.create().write(rBigInteger);` and `ASN1Encoder.create().write(sBigInteger);`) create encoders, write into them and discard the results; the actual DER is produced by the `writeDerSeq(...)` call below with freshly created encoders. These two statements have no effect and only add confusion (a reader may believe the first encoders are the ones serialized). They should be removed.

findings.title: Malformed DER input causes unchecked exceptions instead of IOException
findings.body: `readInteger()` uses the value returned by `readLength()` without validating it. `readLength()` returns `-1` for the indefinite-length form (0x80), so `read(-1)` executes `new byte[-1]` and throws `NegativeArraySizeException`; a zero-length INTEGER (`02 00`) yields an empty array and `new BigInteger(new byte[0])` throws `NumberFormatException` ("Zero length BigInteger"). Both are unchecked exceptions escaping a method declared `throws IOException`, which is what callers of `asn1derToConcatenatedRS` handle. Since the input is an attacker-supplied token signature, this turns a verification failure into an unexpected runtime error propagating out of the verification path. `readInteger()` (and `readNext()`) should reject negative/zero lengths with an `IOException`.

findings.title: Test only round-trips through the new encoder/decoder, so a wrong DER encoding would not be detected
findings.body: The test asserts `asn1der -> concat -> asn1der -> concat` self-consistency using only `AuthzClientCryptoProvider`'s own `ASN1Encoder`/`ASN1Decoder`. If `concatenatedRSToASN1DER` produced structurally wrong DER (wrong tag, wrong length form, missing leading-zero for negative-looking values), the matching custom decoder would still accept it and the assertion would pass. The produced DER should be validated against the JDK, e.g. by calling `Signature.verify(asn1Des)` with the public key (and/or comparing against the BC-based provider output). Additionally, the key pair is created with the JDK default EC curve (P-256) for all three tests, so ES384/ES512 never exercise the real r/s sizes, and the leading-zero-stripping branch of `integerToBytes` (`qLength < bytes.length`) is only hit by chance depending on the randomly generated key; the test should use P-256/P-384/P-521 keys matching each algorithm.

findings.title: getBouncyCastleProvider() returns an unrelated JDK provider, making BouncyIntegration.PROVIDER point to e.g. "SUN"
findings.body: `getBouncyCastleProvider()` returns `KeyStore.getInstance(KeyStore.getDefaultType()).getProvider()`, i.e. typically the JDK's `SUN`/`SunJSSE` provider, although the interface contract states it must return a BouncyCastle (FIPS or non-FIPS) provider. `BouncyIntegration.PROVIDER` is derived from this value, so any keycloak-core code reachable from the authz client that does `Xxx.getInstance(algorithm, BouncyIntegration.PROVIDER)` will be routed to a provider that does not implement the requested algorithms and will fail with a confusing `NoSuchAlgorithmException` instead of the clear `UnsupportedOperationException` the rest of this class raises. Consider returning a provider that actually matches the contract or documenting/handling the null case in `BouncyIntegration` instead of this workaround.
